lesson.title: The No-ge- Club
lesson.subtitle: studiert, never gestudiert — how stress polices the participle

hook.title: The Stress Police
hook.content: German stamps ge- onto almost every past participle: gemacht, gesagt, gekommen. Almost. The -ieren verbs are the club that never pays: studiert, repariert, kopiert — no ge-, ever. The reason is acoustic, not arbitrary: German refuses to put its weak little prefix ge- in front of a syllable that outranks it. Since -ieren verbs stress the suffix (-IE-), the participle simply skips the prefix. You met this club in the -ieren lesson; today you learn its law and spend its earnings.

footnotes.title: The Other Exempt Members
footnotes.content: Verbs starting with an unstressed prefix skip ge- for the same reason: verstanden (understood — ver- is unstressed), besucht (visited). One law everywhere: no unstressed ge- in front of a stronger syllable.

pattern.title: The Perfekt Preview: Bracket + Participle
pattern.content: Put haben in position 2 and the participle closes the bracket — the same frame you mastered with modals: Ich habe Deutsch studiert. Wir haben den Computer repariert. Du hast ein Buch kopiert. In the present it just works: Das System funktioniert. In the past, the bracket returns: Das System hat funktioniert. Every sentence is your modal bracket wearing a past-tense coat: auxiliary opens, participle closes.
pattern.linguist_note: This is the first sighting of the Perfekt bracket, the most common spoken past tense in German. The full ge- participle system arrives later — but -ieren verbs are already ready today: studiert, repariert, kopiert, organisiert, funktioniert.

exercises.explanation: Suffix stress (-IE-) blocks the unstressed ge-: studiert, never gestudiert.

exercises.prompt: Match each -ieren verb with its ge--free participle — the club's newest members included:
exercises.target_answer: repariert, organisiert, kopiert, funktioniert, anprobiert, fotografiert, spaziert
exercises.meaning: repaired, organized, copied, worked, tried on, photographed, gone for a walk
exercises.explanation: Drop -en from the infinitive, add -t — no ge- anywhere in the club, even when a separable prefix rides along: anprobiert keeps its an up front.

exercises.explanation: Stem 'repar-' + '-iert': repariert. The ge- tile stays in the box.

exercises.meaning: Ich habe Deutsch studiert = I have studied German
exercises.explanation: haben opens in position 2, the ge--free participle closes at the end.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "I have repaired the computer"

vocab_hints.note: der Computer takes den in the accusative — the Him-Case again

exercises.explanation: The Perfekt bracket: 'habe' opens, 'repariert' closes — and the computer stays masculine accusative in between.
cues: Start with "Ich" and anchor "habe" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Form ge--free participles of -ieren verbs and build your first Perfekt brackets.
summary.takeaway: Suffix stress exempts -ieren verbs from ge-: studiert, repariert, kopiert — and haben + participle gives you the spoken past for free.

reparieren.context_translation: I have to repair the television.

funktionieren.etymology_derivation: Used specifically for machines and mechanisms functioning properly.

anprobieren.context_translation: I would like to try on the jacket.
anprobieren.etymology_derivation: an- + probieren (to try), from Latin probare - a verb of the French-derived -ieren family; as a separable verb it keeps ge- inside: anprobiert. [wiktionary]

spazieren.english_cognate: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.english_meaning: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian spaziare, from Latin spatiari, to stroll — an -ieren verb; English space is from the same Latin spatium. [wiktionary]

fotografieren.context_translation: We are photographing the old houses.
fotografieren.etymology_derivation: A Greek-rooted international word in the -ieren loan-verb family; like all -ieren verbs its participle takes no ge-: fotografiert. [wiktionary]

danke.etymology_derivation: Ellipsis of ich danke dir — the same danken already known (the think/thank family, th→d). [wiktionary]

golden.etymology_derivation: Gold 'gold' + the suffix -en 'made of' — the page explicitly lists English golden as a cognate (Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz). [wiktionary]

schüssel.context_phrase: Die Schüssel Salat steht auf dem Tisch.
schüssel.context_translation: The bowl of salad is on the table.
schüssel.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic skutilu, an early borrowing of Latin scutella, meaning shallow dish; English scuttle, as in coal scuttle, is the same Latin word through Old English. [wiktionary]

schon.etymology_derivation: Originally the adverb of schön 'beautiful' (Middle High German schōne 'beautifully'); it slid to already, and the page compares English pretty making the same journey. [wiktionary]

supermarkt.context_translation: I buy fruit at the supermarket.
supermarkt.etymology_derivation: super- (above) + Markt (market): the super- is the same Latin prefix English uses, and Markt is the market twin. [wiktionary]

operieren.context_phrase: Der Arzt operiert den Patienten heute.
operieren.context_translation: The doctor operates on the patient today.
operieren.etymology_derivation: From Latin operari, to work, plus the -ieren suffix — the standard Latin-loan verb pattern, exactly like operate; the participle is operiert with no ge- prefix. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
